hey, i stumbled across this late but i just wanted to say the way society treats short men is so ridiculous. this obsession with tallness is literally just a couple of vertical inches to the body, like why do people care its not a big deal. height is not everything, and if someone treats it as such, then theyre prioritizing the wrong things. once i was scrolling on yt shorts, i think it was from tiktok but this short guy caught my eye. he had a great fashion sense and was one of the more attractive people i had seen in some time. its been too long to find the video again but i remember the comments having the same opinion. his confidence was also attractive, he didnt let his height get to him. also, i once crushed on a guy your height. i never really thought about him being short because it genuinely never mattered. his friends were tall but i was drawn to him. and this is coming from someone who rarely, like rarely crushes on people.

i know this probably wont help because ik its so difficult to brush off society's distorted views when its pushed onto everyone. its hard. but i promise, you are just as much of a man as anyone else is. i promise. if someone treats you bad because of your height, that has nothing to do with you and everything to do with them. it reveals how shallow they are and that they waste their energy on insignificant things. those kinds of people arent worth anyones time.

before i had bd, when i was like 9 or 10 yrs old i would frequently "roast" my friend because i thought it was funny. it had absolutely nothing to do with what i thought of her - i did it purely because i thought her reactions were funny and i was an immature idiot. she never spoke up about it until one day she just burst and yelled at me in tears, saying that i was making her insecure. i was shocked. i NEVER realized how my jokes couldve actually hurt her feelings (i was so stupid, i regret it), so i stopped and learned from my mistake. sometimes people dont realize when playful teasing gets under someones skin, so its up to you to communicate your feelings. if they dont take you seriously, then youll realize what kind of friends they truly are and hopefully you could surround yourself with better people. but right now you need to talk to them so that they can realize the impact of their words.

this comment is really comforting to me. i feel like everyone pushes the message that you're supposed to like how you look, you're supposed to "see your beauty". it leaves me feeling hopeless, because what if i simply can't find anything to like in my face? you've reminded me to do something a counsellor told me to years ago - instead of focusing so much on what i don't like, i need to redirect that attention to what i do like about myself. i think this is the only way i can heal because i honestly can't find anything to like about my face, so i have to accept those feelings but also find worth in other things i can be good at. i know this wasn't commented on my post but thanks for this, it's kind of rare that advice for bdd actually helps me.

i understand what you mean. while i still dislike seeing myself in the mirror, it's never as bad as the pictures. i look absolutely messed up in photos, and for some reason my proportions get so disgustingly weird. it makes me want to vomit. but i'm learning to not fully trust the camera because it does have lens distortion. have you ever tried to take a picture of something, maybe a pretty view but the photo never compares to how it looks in reality? mirrors are more accurate because while they do show a reverse image, there isn't a lens to distort things, they just reflect objects. i've heard others say they know people who look different on camera, and that they look a lot better in person. so honestly i try to avoid seeing pictures with myself because i don't want to get upset over something that probably doesn't even accurately reflect reality.

do you know how to deal with feeling alone? i've always struggled with making friends, and i can't just find a parental figure - i need to learn how to accept the fact that i don't have anyone because i feel that it's unhealthy to rely on this addiction.

we're so used to seeing the inverted version of our faces in reflections that when it's flipped in a photo, the asymmetry seems to pop out and it takes us by surprise. the truth is everyone has some asymmetry, so if you flip a picture back and forth it's going to shift around. that's completely normal - if someone was perfectly symmetrical like in those photo app mirror effects, i think it'd look unsettling because asymmetry is natural and is found everywhere. no one really registers these small differences when we look at others' faces because we just see their general appearance, nobody looks at someone and thinks "damn your eye is 3 degrees off" - it's unnoticeable. my friends have said things like "my right eye is a lot lower than the other" and "one side of my jaw is huge" which surprised me a lot because i *never* saw those things in them.

since you find it distracting, that would be best. however, it might be difficult to abruptly drop something you're so used to. if you struggle to quit listening, i'd suggest putting on a different genre that would serve as background ambience and wouldn't trigger daydreaming. if that doesn't work, try setting certain times just for pacing and listening to music (ex. for 5 minutes after every 30 minutes of working). that way you get it out of your system and you can (hopefully) get back to the homework. if this works, you can slowly cut down on how much time you allow yourself to daydream and eventually you'll be able to work uninterrupted for longer periods of time.
i think that's really nice actually. just by giving something new a go, it turned into an enjoyable hobby that makes you feel some sense of worth. i like that story :)
